> Each group picks a question about one of two new datasets, works on it over two
> mornings, and on Friday presents to a group that worked on the other dataset.
> We do not give you an answer to check against.

## Groups and schedule

There are ten groups of six people. Five groups (A1 to A5) take Study A and five
(B1 to B5) take Study B. You meet your group on Wednesday morning.

On Friday each Study A group pairs with the Study B group of the same number and
sits with them. A1 presents to B1, then B1 presents to A1; A2 and B2 do the same
nearby, and so on. Your audience has spent two mornings on a different dataset,
so explain your study before your result.

| when | how long | what |
|---|---|---|
| Wednesday AM | 3 hours | meet, read the data, agree a question, first analysis: Tuesday's ordination and PERMANOVA are a good place to start |
| Thursday AM | 3 hours | add Wednesday's differential tests, finish the analysis, build the figures, write the talk |
| Friday AM | 30 minutes | final preparation |
| Friday AM | 1 hour | present to your paired group for 30 minutes, then listen to theirs for 30 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,16,66]"}

Both datasets have exactly the file layout you have been using all week, with the
same column names. Your code from the modules should run on them with the file
path changed and nothing else.

```r
source("R/count_tables.R")
d <- read_counts("group_a")   # or "group_b"
```

## Study A: does a vaginal probiotic change the community?

A randomised trial. Participants received either a live *Lactobacillus crispatus*
product or a placebo, and were sampled before and after the course of treatment.

| | |
|---|---|
| participants | 176 |
| samples | 352, one before and one after per person |
| arms | 121 probiotic, 55 placebo |
| metadata | `arm`, `time_point` (`pre`, `post`), age, pH, Nugent score, Amsel criteria |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

The obvious question is whether the product changed the bacterial community, and
whether it changed host gene expression.

There are less obvious ones. Did it work in everyone, or only in people whose
community was already a particular way before treatment? Does the host response
track the community change, or move on its own? Is a difference after treatment
meaningful if the two arms already differed before it?

The arms are unbalanced, 121 against 55, so check your baseline before you
interpret anything about the follow-up.

## Study B: do hormonal contraceptives differ in their effect?

A cross-sectional comparison of three contraceptive methods, each person sampled
once.

| | |
|---|---|
| participants | 93, one sample each |
| arms | 39 injectable, 28 pill, 26 ring |
| metadata | `arm`, `bv` (Amsel), `nugent`, `ph`, `any_sti` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

The obvious question is whether the three methods differ in bacterial community
composition, in host gene expression, or in both.

Then the less obvious ones. One of the three methods is delivered locally and two
are systemic. Does that grouping explain more than the three-way split does? Is
bacterial vaginosis more common in one arm, and if so is that the explanation for
everything else you find? With 93 samples and three groups, which of your
comparisons is actually powered?

Keep in mind that the study is cross-sectional. Nobody was randomised to a
method, and people who choose different methods differ in other ways.

## Deliverables

A presentation that fits your 30-minute slot, containing:

1. the question you settled on, in one sentence
2. what you did, including what you filtered and why
3. two or three figures, each with a caption you read out
4. the answer, stated as plainly as the data allow
5. what you do not believe about your own result

The last of these is required. When you are the audience, ask the other group
about theirs. Every
analysis this week had something wrong with it, so look for the problems in
yours before you present.

## Advice from the modules

::: {.callout-tip}
## Things that bit people earlier in the week

- Check your sample table and your count matrix are in the same order before you
  run any test.
- Decide your filter before you look at the result, and write down why.
- On a species table, give DESeq2 `poscounts` size factors and check how many
  species they were built from.
- Define a grouping from one table and test the other, never the same table
  twice.
- Look at how lopsided a ranking is before you believe an enrichment.
- Your dataset has an `rnaseq_batch` column. Cross-tabulate it against your
  groups early, and find out whether you have a confound rather than a finding.
:::

## Using the agent

Use Pi as much as you like. It writes most code faster than you can, and groups
that use it well tend to get further.

At some point this week it will also give you an answer that is confident and
wrong.
Before any number goes on a slide, one person in the group who did not write the
code should be able to say where it came from.

Divide the work: someone drives the analysis, someone checks it, someone builds
the figures, someone writes the talk. Swap at least once.
